narration.full_text: Let's work through an example to see how trigonometric ratios can help us prove angle equality. We're given that B and Q are acute angles, and that the sine of angle B is equal to the sine of angle Q. Our goal is to prove that angle B is equal to angle Q. To do this, we'll consider two right-angled triangles, triangle ABC and triangle PQR. In triangle ABC, angle C is the right angle, and in triangle PQR, angle R is the right angle. We know that sine B is the ratio of the opposite side AC to the hypotenuse AB. Similarly, sine Q is the ratio of the opposite side PR to the hypotenuse PQ. Since sine B equals sine Q, we can set these ratios equal to each other. This means that the ratio of AC to PR is equal to the ratio of AB to PQ. Let's call this common ratio 'k'. Next, we'll use the Pythagorean theorem to find the length of the adjacent sides, BC and QR. For triangle ABC, BC is the square root of AB squared minus AC squared. And for triangle PQR, QR is the square root of PQ squared minus PR squared. By substituting our 'k' relationship from earlier, we can show that the ratio of BC to QR is also equal to 'k'. Since all three corresponding side ratios are equal to 'k', we can conclude that triangle ABC is similar to triangle PQR. And because similar triangles have corresponding angles that are equal, we can confidently state that angle B is indeed equal to angle Q. This demonstrates how the equality of sine ratios directly implies the equality of the angles themselves, provided they are acute.
